title: Variational inference
text: The posterior of an unobserved quantity is often too hard to compute. Variational inference replaces it with a simpler stand-in that is close to it, where closeness is measured by the KL divergence.

title: Variational inference
text:
1 The evidence lower bound








Definition 1 (Evidence lower bound (ELBO)) Let \(x\) be observed data, and let \(z\) be an unobserved discrete random variable, with joint probability mass function \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\). Let \(q\) be a probability mass function for \(z\). Require that \(q\) gives probability zero to every value \(z\) where the posterior \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(z \mid x\right)\mathclose{}}\) is zero. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) of \(q\) is the average, over \(z\) drawn from \(q\), of the difference between the logarithm of \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\) and the logarithm of \(q(z)\):
\[\mathrm{ELBO}(q) = {\mathbb{E}_{q}\mathopen{}\left[{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}}.\]
Written as a sum over the values \(z\) with \(q(z) > 0\), the average is
\[\mathrm{ELBO}(q) = \sum_z q(z) \mathopen{}\left({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}.\]











Theorem 1 (The log evidence is the ELBO plus a divergence) Let \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\) and \(q\) be as in Definition 1. Let \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = \sum_z {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\) be the evidence of the data, also called its marginal likelihood. The evidence is nonzero, because a data value \(x\) was observed. Then the logarithm of the evidence is the ELBO of \(q\) plus the Kullback–Leibler divergence of \(q\) from the posterior:
\[{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} = \mathrm{ELBO}(q) + {{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(q \,\Vert\, {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(\cdot \mid x\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(z\) be a value with \(q(z) > 0\). Then \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(z \mid x\right)\mathclose{}} \ne 0\), and \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(z \mid x\right)\mathclose{}} \, {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\). Apply \(\operatorname{log}\) to both sides and rearrange:
\[{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(z \mid x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}.\]
Add and subtract \({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) on the right:
\[{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} = \mathopen{}\left({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(z \mid x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}.\]
Multiply both sides by \(q(z)\), then sum over the values \(z\) with \(q(z) > 0\). The left side sums to \({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because \(q\) sums to \(1\):
\[{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} = \sum_z q(z) \mathopen{}\left({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x, z\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{} + \sum_z q(z) \mathopen{}\left({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{q(z)\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(z \mid x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}.\]
The first sum is \(\mathrm{ELBO}(q)\) by its definition. The second sum is \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(q \,\Vert\, {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(\cdot \mid x\right)\mathclose{}}\right)\mathclose{}}\) by the definition of the divergence.











Example 1 (The ELBO and the divergence for a three-valued latent variable)  

Let \(z\) take the values \(1, 2, 3\) with prior probabilities \(0.5, 0.3, 0.2\). A data value \(x\) is observed, and its probabilities given \(z\) are \(0.1, 0.4, 0.8\). The R chunk below finds the posterior, then computes the ELBO and the divergence for three choices of \(q\), with natural logarithms.


Show code
prior <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
likelihood <- c(0.1, 0.4, 0.8)
joint <- prior * likelihood
evidence <- sum(joint)
posterior <- joint / evidence
log_evidence <- log(evidence)

elbo_and_divergence <- function(q) {
  log_ratio <- log(joint) - log(q)
  elbo <- sum(q * log_ratio)
  log_gap <- log(q) - log(posterior)
  divergence <- sum(q * log_gap)
  c(elbo = elbo, divergence = divergence, total = elbo + divergence)
}

uniform <- rep(1 / 3, 3)
shifted <- c(0.2, 0.3, 0.5)
rows <- rbind(
  uniform = elbo_and_divergence(uniform),
  shifted = elbo_and_divergence(shifted),
  posterior = elbo_and_divergence(posterior)
)
round(rows, 4)
#>              elbo divergence   total
#> uniform   -1.2176     0.1089 -1.1087
#> shifted   -1.1219     0.0132 -1.1087
#> posterior -1.1087     0.0000 -1.1087


The evidence is \(0.33\), so its logarithm is \(-1.1087\). In every row the ELBO plus the divergence equals this value, as Theorem 1 says. The ELBO is largest, and the divergence is \(0\), for \(q\) equal to the posterior.











Remark 1 (Variational inference maximizes the ELBO). The logarithm of the evidence \({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) does not depend on \(q\). By Theorem 1, choosing \(q\) to maximize the ELBO is therefore the same as choosing \(q\) to minimize its Kullback–Leibler divergence from the posterior. The ELBO never exceeds the logarithm of the evidence, because the divergence is at least \(0\). Variational inference searches a restricted family of choices for \(q\) this way (Blei et al. 2017).

title: Source coding
text:
Definition 1 (Binary code) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. A binary code for \(X\) assigns each value \(x\) a codeword, a string of \(\ell(x)\) bits.











Definition 2 (Uniquely decodable code) A binary code is uniquely decodable if every finite sequence of codewords, written one after another, can be split back into codewords in only one way.











Definition 3 (Expected length) The expected length of a binary code for a discrete random variable \(X\) is the expectation of its codeword length:
\[L \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\ell(X)\right]\mathclose{}}.\]











Theorem 1 (Expected length as a sum over values) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable with probability mass function \(p(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathbb{P}(X=x)\). The expected length of a binary code for \(X\) is
\[L = \sum_{x} p(x) \, \ell(x).\]










ProofProof






Proof. The codeword length \(\ell(X)\) is a random variable whose possible values are the codeword lengths \(\ell(x)\). By the definition of expectation,
\[L = \sum_{k} k \, \mathbb{P}(\ell(X) = k).\]
The event \(\ell(X) = k\) is the union of the disjoint events \(X = x\) over the values \(x\) with \(\ell(x) = k\). So \(\mathbb{P}(\ell(X) = k) = \sum_{x : \ell(x) = k} p(x)\), and
\[L = \sum_{k} \sum_{x : \ell(x) = k} k \, p(x).\]
On the inner sum \(k = \ell(x)\). Every value \(x\) lies in exactly one inner sum, so the double sum runs once over each value:
\[L = \sum_{x} \ell(x) \, p(x).\]











Example 1 (Expected length of a code for a three-valued variable)  

Let \(X\) have probability mass function \(p = (1/2, 1/4, 1/4)\), and let a binary code for \(X\) have codeword lengths \(\ell = (1, 2, 2)\). The code below computes the expected length from its definition, as the expectation of \(\ell(X)\), and as the sum in Theorem 1.


Show code
p <- c(1 / 2, 1 / 4, 1 / 4)
len <- c(1, 2, 2)
lengths_seen <- sort(unique(len))
prob_of_length <- vapply(
  lengths_seen,
  function(k) sum(p[len == k]),
  numeric(1)
)
from_definition <- sum(lengths_seen * prob_of_length)
from_sum <- sum(p * len)
c(from_definition = from_definition, from_sum = from_sum)
#> from_definition        from_sum 
#>             1.5             1.5


Both give \(L = 1.5\) bits, as Theorem 1 states.











Remark 1 (Short codewords for common values). A code with a small expected length gives frequent values short codewords and rare values long ones, since each value’s \(\ell(x)\) counts in \(L\) weighted by its probability.

title: Source coding
text:
2 The source coding theorem








Theorem 2 (Source coding theorem) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable that takes a finite number of values, at least two of them with nonzero probability, and let \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) be its entropy with base-2 logarithms.

Every uniquely decodable binary code for \(X\) has expected length \(L \ge {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\).
Some uniquely decodable binary code for \(X\) has expected length \(L < {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} + 1\).
Coding \(n\) independent copies of \(X\) at a time, some uniquely decodable binary code spends, on average, fewer than \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} + 1/n\) bits per copy.












Remark 2 (Where the theorem comes from). Shannon (1948) proved that no compression of the output of a source can beat its entropy. Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 5.3 to 5.5) prove each part of Theorem 2. For part 2, they give each value \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\) the length \(\ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil\), its surprisal in bits rounded up; Kraft’s condition (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 5.2) guarantees that there is a code with these lengths.

title: Source coding
text:
3 Coding with the wrong distribution








Theorem 3 (The cost of coding with the wrong distribution) Let \(X\) take a finite number of values, with probability mass function \(p\), and let \(q\) be such a function, possibly different from \(p\), with \(q(x) > 0\) wherever \(p(x) > 0\). Suppose a code gives each value \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\) the length \(\ell(x) = \lceil -\log_2 q(x) \rceil\). Then its expected length \(L\) under \(p\) satisfies
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}} \le L < {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}} + 1,\]
where \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}}\) is the cross-entropy of \(q\) relative to \(p\), with base-2 logarithms.










ProofProof






Proof. Every sum here runs over the values \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\). Rounding up adds less than one binary digit, so for each such \(x\)
\[-\log_2 q(x) \le \ell(x) < -\log_2 q(x) + 1.\]
Multiply each part by \(p(x) > 0\) and sum. Since \(\sum_{x} p(x) = 1\),
\[
-\sum_{x} p(x) \log_2 q(x)
\le \sum_{x} p(x) \, \ell(x)
< -\sum_{x} p(x) \log_2 q(x) + 1.
\]
The middle sum is \(L\) by Theorem 1, and the outer sums are \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}}\).











Theorem 4 (Cross-entropy is entropy plus divergence) Let \(p\) and \(q\) be probability mass functions on the values \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\), with \(q(x) > 0\) wherever \(p(x) > 0\). Write \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}}\) for the entropy of \(p\), \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}}\) for the cross-entropy of \(q\) relative to \(p\), and \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(p \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}}\) for the Kullback–Leibler divergence of \(q\) from \(p\), all with base-2 logarithms. Then
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}} + {{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(p \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Every sum here runs over the values \(x\) with \(p(x) > 0\). For every such \(x\),
\[
-\log_2 q(x)
= -\log_2 p(x) + \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\]
Multiply by \(p(x)\) and add over \(x\):
\[
-\sum_x p(x) \log_2 q(x)
= -\sum_x p(x) \log_2 p(x) + \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\]
Reading left to right, these are \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}}\) and \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(p \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}}\).











Example 2 (Cross-entropy, entropy and divergence for a uniform code)  

Let \(p = (1/2, 1/4, 1/4)\) be the probability mass function of a three-valued random variable, and let \(q = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)\) assign \(1/3\) to each of the three values. The code below computes the cross-entropy, the entropy and the divergence in bits.


Show code
p <- c(1 / 2, 1 / 4, 1 / 4)
q <- rep(1 / 3, 3)
cross_entropy <- -sum(p * log2(q))
shannon_entropy <- -sum(p * log2(p))
divergence <- sum(p * log2(p / q))
c(
  cross_entropy = cross_entropy,
  shannon_entropy = shannon_entropy,
  divergence = divergence
)
#>   cross_entropy shannon_entropy      divergence 
#>       1.5849625       1.5000000       0.0849625


The cross-entropy is \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}} = 1.585\) bits. The entropy is \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}} = 1.5\) bits, and the divergence is \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(p \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}} = 0.085\) bits. They satisfy Theorem 4: 1.5 + 0.085 = 1.585.











Remark 3 (Cross-entropy is the cost of the wrong code). Theorem 4 splits the cross-entropy into the entropy and the divergence. By Theorem 2, no uniquely decodable code averages fewer than \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}}\) bits. By Theorem 3, a code built for \(q\) costs about \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(p \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}}\) bits per value more than that. By the divergence theorem, the excess vanishes only when the code was built for \(p\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 2.6; Yeung 2008, sec. 2.5). Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 5.4) state Theorem 3 in this form, with \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p\right)\mathclose{}} + {{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(p \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}}\) in place of \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(p, q\right)\mathclose{}}\).











Remark 4 (Why models are fit by minimizing cross-entropy). Fitting a classifier by minimizing cross-entropy chooses the probabilities \(q\) the model assigns so that a code built for \(q\) would spend as few bits as possible on the observed labels. By Remark 3, that pushes \(q\) toward the probabilities the labels came from.
For a single labeled example, let \(e\) put all its mass on the observed label. Then \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(e\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\) (as for a coin that always lands heads), so the example’s cross-entropy \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(e, q\right)\mathclose{}}\) equals \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(e \,\Vert\, q\right)\mathclose{}}\): every bit it reports is a wasted one.

title: Perfect secrecy
text: A cipher hides a message from an eavesdropper who sees only the ciphertext. Mutual information says exactly how much the ciphertext can reveal, and so how much key a cipher needs.

title: Perfect secrecy
text:
1 Perfect secrecy








Definition 1 (Perfect secrecy) Let \(M\) be a message, let \(K\) be a key independent of \(M\), and let \(C\) be the ciphertext made from \(M\) and \(K\), all discrete random variables with finite entropies. The key and the ciphertext together determine the message. The cipher has perfect secrecy when the ciphertext tells an eavesdropper nothing about the message, that is, when \(M\) and \(C\) have zero mutual information:
\[{\mathbb{I}\mathopen{}\left(M ; C\right)\mathclose{}} = 0.\]
The definition is from (Shannon 1949).











Example 1 (The one-time pad with a two-bit message)  

Let the message take the four values \(0, 1, 2, 3\) (two bits) with probabilities \(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1\). The key is uniform on the same four values, and the ciphertext is the bitwise exclusive or of message and key. The R chunk below builds the joint distribution of message and ciphertext, and computes the mutual information between them.


Show code
prior <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)
joint <- matrix(0, nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
for (m in 0:3) {
  for (k in 0:3) {
    c_value <- bitwXor(m, k)
    joint[m + 1, c_value + 1] <- joint[m + 1, c_value + 1] + prior[m + 1] / 4
  }
}
cipher_prob <- colSums(joint)
product <- outer(prior, cipher_prob)
max_gap <- max(abs(joint - product))
mutual_info <- sum(joint * log2(joint / product))
c(max_gap = max_gap, mutual_info = mutual_info)
#>     max_gap mutual_info 
#>           0           0


The ciphertext is uniform, with probability \(0.25\) on each value, and the largest gap between the joint distribution and the product of the two marginal distributions is \(0\). So the mutual information is \(0\) bits: the pad has perfect secrecy for these message probabilities.











Theorem 1 (Perfect secrecy needs a key with at least the entropy of the message) Let \(M\), \(K\) and \(C\) be as in Definition 1, and suppose the cipher has perfect secrecy. Then the entropy of the key is at least the entropy of the message:
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K\right)\mathclose{}} \ge {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M\right)\mathclose{}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition 1, \({\mathbb{I}\mathopen{}\left(M ; C\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\), so \(M\) and \(C\) are independent, and the equality case of conditioning reduces entropy gives the first step:
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M \mid C\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
The chain rule expands both conditional entropies below:
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M \mid C\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M, C\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(C\right)\mathclose{}}, \qquad {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K \mid C\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K, C\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(C\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
Apply the chain rule to \((M, C)\) and \(K\) jointly in two orders:
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M, C, K\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(C, K\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M \mid C, K\right)\mathclose{}}, \qquad {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M, C, K\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M, C\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K \mid M, C\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
The key and the ciphertext determine the message, so \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M \mid C, K\right)\mathclose{}} = 0\). A conditional entropy is nonnegative, so \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K \mid M, C\right)\mathclose{}} \ge 0\). Equating the two expansions then gives \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M, C\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(C, K\right)\mathclose{}}\). Subtract \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(C\right)\mathclose{}}\) from both sides:
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M \mid C\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K \mid C\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
By conditioning reduces entropy again, \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K \mid C\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K\right)\mathclose{}}\). Chain the three comparisons:
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(M \mid C\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K \mid C\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(K\right)\mathclose{}}.\]











Example 2 (The key of a one-time pad is as long as the message)  

The R chunk below computes the entropy of the message and of the key of Example 1.


Show code
prior <- c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)
key_prob <- rep(1 / 4, 4)
message_entropy <- -sum(prior * log2(prior))
key_entropy <- -sum(key_prob * log2(key_prob))
c(message_entropy = message_entropy, key_entropy = key_entropy)
#> message_entropy     key_entropy 
#>        1.846439        2.000000


The message has \(1.846\) bits of entropy, and the key has \(2\) bits, so the key’s entropy is at least the message’s, as Theorem 1 requires. A key with fewer than \(1.846\) bits of entropy could not give this message perfect secrecy.











Remark 1 (Source of the definition and the theorem). Perfect secrecy and the theorem on the key are from (Shannon 1949). The proof above uses only the chain rule and conditioning reduces entropy, both of which are results about entropy.

title: Min-entropy
text: The entropy of a random variable averages its surprisal. Other summaries of its probabilities answer other questions. This page adds the smallest of them, the min-entropy, to the collision entropy.

title: Min-entropy
text:
1 Min-entropy








Definition 1 (Min-entropy) The min-entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the logarithm of the reciprocal of the largest probability that \(X\) takes any one value:
\[{\mathbb{H}_{\infty}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = -\log \max_x {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
It is the limiting case of the Rényi entropy of order \(\alpha\) (Rényi 1961), which approaches it as \(\alpha \to \infty\).











Example 1 (Min-entropy of a three-valued random variable)  

Let \(X\) take three values with probabilities \(1/2\), \(1/4\) and \(1/4\). The R chunk below finds the largest probability and the min-entropy, with base-2 logarithms.


Show code
p <- c(1 / 2, 1 / 4, 1 / 4)
max_prob <- max(p)
min_entropy <- -log2(max_prob)
c(max_prob = max_prob, min_entropy = min_entropy)
#>    max_prob min_entropy 
#>         0.5         1.0


The largest probability is \(0.5\), so the min-entropy is \({\mathbb{H}_{\infty}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = 1\) bit.











Theorem 1 (The min-entropy is at most the collision entropy) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. Then the min-entropy is at most the collision entropy:
\[{\mathbb{H}_{\infty}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}_{2}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(p_{\max} = \max_x {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}\). Each probability \({\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}\) is at most \(p_{\max}\), so \({\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}^2 \le p_{\max} \, {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}\). Sum over the values \(x\):
\[\sum_x {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}^2 \le p_{\max} \sum_x {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
The probabilities sum to \(1\), so the collision probability is at most \(p_{\max}\):
\[\mathbb{P}(X = X') = \sum_x {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X = x\right)\mathclose{}}^2 \le p_{\max}.\]
The function \(-\log\) is decreasing, so taking it of both sides flips the comparison:
\[-\log \mathbb{P}(X = X') \ge -\log p_{\max}.\]
The left side is \({\mathbb{H}_{2}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) and the right side is \({\mathbb{H}_{\infty}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\).











Example 2 (Three entropies of one random variable)  

The R chunk below computes the min-entropy, the collision entropy and the entropy of the random variable of Example 1.


Show code
p <- c(1 / 2, 1 / 4, 1 / 4)
min_entropy <- -log2(max(p))
collision_entropy <- -log2(sum(p^2))
shannon_entropy <- -sum(p * log2(p))
c(
  min_entropy = min_entropy,
  collision_entropy = collision_entropy,
  shannon_entropy = shannon_entropy
)
#>       min_entropy collision_entropy   shannon_entropy 
#>          1.000000          1.415037          1.500000


The values rise from \(1\) to \(1.415\) to \(1.5\) bits, as Theorem 1 and the collision entropy bound say.











Remark 1 (Min-entropy measures the chance of a single guess). The best single guess at the value of \(X\) is its most probable value, and that guess is right with probability \(2^{-{\mathbb{H}_{\infty}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}}\). So a min-entropy of \(k\) bits says that no guess succeeds with probability above \(2^{-k}\). The entropy gives no such guarantee, because it can be large while one value is very likely. That is why min-entropy is the measure of a secret’s unpredictability.

title: KL divergence and maximum likelihood
text: The Kullback–Leibler divergence of one model from another is the number of bits per value that a code built for the model wastes, by the cross-entropy decomposition. This page applies that to data, and shows that the model a maximum likelihood estimate picks is the model with the least waste.

title: KL divergence and maximum likelihood
text:
1 Maximum likelihood








Theorem 1 (Maximum likelihood minimizes the divergence from the data) Let \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) be data, and let \(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits\) be their empirical distribution. Let \(q_\theta\) be probability mass functions with \(q_\theta(v) > 0\) wherever \(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits(v) > 0\), for parameter values \(\theta\). Then \(\theta\) maximizes the likelihood \(\prod_{i=1}^n q_\theta(x_i)\) exactly when it minimizes the Kullback–Leibler divergence \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits \,\Vert\, q_\theta\right)\mathclose{}}\).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(n_v\) be the number of data equal to \(v\). Then \(n_v = n \, \mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits(v)\).
Group the terms of the log-likelihood by value:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \log_2 q_\theta(x_i) = \sum_v n \, \mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits(v) \log_2 q_\theta(v).\]
Divide by \(n\). The right side is minus the cross-entropy \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits, q_\theta\right)\mathclose{}}\):
\[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log_2 q_\theta(x_i) = -{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits, q_\theta\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
By the cross-entropy decomposition, the cross-entropy is the entropy of \(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits\) plus the divergence:
\[-{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits, q_\theta\right)\mathclose{}} = -{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits\right)\mathclose{}} - {{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits \,\Vert\, q_\theta\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
The entropy \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits\right)\mathclose{}}\) does not depend on \(\theta\). So \(\theta\) maximizes the average log-likelihood exactly when it minimizes \({{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\mathopen{}\left(\mathop{\hat{\mathbb{p}}}\nolimits \,\Vert\, q_\theta\right)\mathclose{}}\). The logarithm increases, and dividing by \(n\) keeps the order, so \(\theta\) maximizes the average log-likelihood exactly when it maximizes the likelihood.











Example 1 (The divergence from the data for coin flips)  

A coin is flipped \(100\) times, and it lands heads \(70\) times. The chunk below follows Theorem 1 for the Bernoulli models with the probability of heads \(0.1, 0.2, \ldots, 0.9\). It prints the divergence of each model from the empirical distribution, the average log-likelihood, and minus the entropy of the empirical distribution minus the divergence.


Show code
n_flips <- 100
n_heads <- 70
empirical <- c(tails = n_flips - n_heads, heads = n_heads) / n_flips
success_prob <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
empirical_entropy <- -sum(empirical * log2(empirical))
divergence <- numeric(length(success_prob))
avg_loglik <- numeric(length(success_prob))
for (j in seq_along(success_prob)) {
  model <- c(1 - success_prob[j], success_prob[j])
  divergence[j] <- sum(empirical * log2(empirical / model))
  avg_loglik[j] <- sum(empirical * log2(model))
}
decomposition <- -empirical_entropy - divergence
data.frame(
  success_prob,
  divergence = round(divergence, 4),
  avg_loglik = round(avg_loglik, 4),
  decomposition = round(decomposition, 4)
)



  



The last two columns agree, as the proof says. The divergence is smallest, at \(0\) bits, and the average log-likelihood is largest for the model with probability of heads \(0.7\), which is the fraction of heads in the data, so that model is the empirical distribution.











Remark 1 (One labeled example). For a single labeled example, \(n = 1\), and the empirical distribution puts all its mass on the observed label. Then Theorem 1 says that the model with the largest probability for that label is the model with the smallest divergence from it. That is the case that the cross-entropy loss remark describes.

title: Huffman codes
text: Source coding shows that the entropy of a source is the least average length of a code for it, up to one bit. This page asks which codes a decoder can read one codeword at a time, and how long such a code must be.

title: Huffman codes
text:
1 Prefix codes








Definition 1 (Prefix code) A binary code for a discrete random variable \(X\) is a prefix code, also called a prefix-free code or an instantaneous code, if no codeword is the beginning of another codeword. Writing \(c(x)\) for the codeword of the value \(x\), the condition is that, for every two different values \(x\) and \(x'\), the string \(c(x')\) does not start with the string \(c(x)\).











Theorem 1 (Kraft’s inequality) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable that takes a finite number of values, and let a prefix code for \(X\) have codeword lengths \(\ell(x)\). Then
\[{s_{x}} 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(m\) be the largest codeword length. It is finite because \(X\) takes a finite number of values.
For each value \(x\), the strings of \(m\) bits that start with the codeword \(c(x)\) are those that choose the remaining \(m - \ell(x)\) bits freely. So there are \(2^{m - \ell(x)}\) of them.
No string of \(m\) bits starts with two different codewords. If it started with \(c(x)\) and with \(c(x')\), where \(\ell(x) \le \ell(x')\), then \(c(x)\) would be the first \(\ell(x)\) bits of \(c(x')\), which the prefix code forbids. So the strings that start with different codewords form groups with no string in two groups.
There are \(2^m\) strings of \(m\) bits in all, so the groups together hold at most that many:
\[{s_{x}} 2^{m - \ell(x)} \le 2^m.\]
Dividing both sides by \(2^m\) gives the claim.











Theorem 2 (Prefix codes exist for lengths that satisfy Kraft’s inequality) Let \(\ell_1 \le \ell_2 \le \cdots \le \ell_n\) be positive integers with
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2^{-\ell_i} \le 1.\]
Then some prefix code on \(n\) values has codeword lengths \(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_n\).










ProofProof






Proof. For each \(i\), let
\[a_i = {s_{j < i}} 2^{-\ell_j},\]
so that \(a_1 = 0\). Let the codeword \(c_i\) be the \(\ell_i\) bits that spell \(N_i = 2^{\ell_i} a_i\) as a base-2 number, with zeros added at the front to reach \(\ell_i\) digits.
This is possible if \(N_i\) is an integer with \(0 \le N_i < 2^{\ell_i}\). Each term of \(N_i = {s_{j < i}} 2^{\ell_i - \ell_j}\) is an integer, because \(\ell_j \le \ell_i\). By the assumption, \(a_i + 2^{-\ell_i} \le {s_{j \le i}} 2^{-\ell_j} \le 1\), so \(N_i \le 2^{\ell_i} - 1 < 2^{\ell_i}\).
Suppose that \(c_i\) were the beginning of \(c_k\) for some \(i < k\). The first \(\ell_i\) digits of \(c_k\) are the base-2 digits of the integer part of \(N_k / 2^{\ell_k - \ell_i} = 2^{\ell_i} a_k\). Because \(c_i\) is these digits, this integer part is \(N_i\).
But \(a_k = a_i + {s_{i \le j < k}} 2^{-\ell_j} \ge a_i + 2^{-\ell_i}\), so \(2^{\ell_i} a_k \ge N_i + 1\), and the integer part of \(2^{\ell_i} a_k\) is at least \(N_i + 1\), not \(N_i\). This contradiction shows that no \(c_i\) with \(i < k\) begins \(c_k\). Nor can \(c_k\) be the beginning of \(c_i\) with \(i < k\): that would give \(\ell_k \le \ell_i\), so \(\ell_k = \ell_i\) and \(c_k = c_i\), which the first case excludes.











Example 1 (A prefix code and a code that is not)  

Take four values with the codeword lengths \((1, 2, 3, 3)\). The code \(0, 10, 110, 111\) is a prefix code. The code \(0, 01, 011, 111\) has the same lengths, but the codeword \(01\) starts with the codeword \(0\), so it is not a prefix code. The code below tests the definition on every pair of codewords, and adds up \(2^{-\ell(x)}\) for each code, as in Theorem 1.


Show code
is_prefix_code <- function(codewords) {
  index <- seq_along(codewords)
  pairs <- expand.grid(shorter = index, longer = index)
  distinct_pairs <- pairs[pairs$shorter != pairs$longer, ]
  shorter_words <- codewords[distinct_pairs$shorter]
  longer_words <- codewords[distinct_pairs$longer]
  begins <- startsWith(longer_words, shorter_words)
  !any(begins)
}
kraft_sum <- function(codewords) {
  lengths <- nchar(codewords)
  sum(2^(-lengths))
}
prefix_code <- c("0", "10", "110", "111")
other_code <- c("0", "01", "011", "111")
codes <- list(prefix_code, other_code)
data.frame(
  code = c("0, 10, 110, 111", "0, 01, 011, 111"),
  is_prefix_code = vapply(codes, is_prefix_code, logical(1)),
  kraft_sum = vapply(codes, kraft_sum, numeric(1))
)



  



Both codes have \({s_{x}} 2^{-\ell(x)} = 1\), the largest value Theorem 1 allows. The sum depends on the lengths alone, so it is the same for the second code, which is not a prefix code. Theorem 2 gives a prefix code with these lengths, and the first code is one.











Remark 1 (Where Kraft’s inequality comes from). Cover and Thomas (2006, sec. 5.2) prove Theorem 1 and Theorem 2. They show in section 5.5 that the lengths of every uniquely decodable code have the same sum at most \(1\), so restricting to prefix codes costs nothing in expected length. MacKay (2003, sec. 5.2) states the result for prefix codes as well.

title: Huffman codes
text:
2 The Huffman algorithm








Definition 2 (Huffman code) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable that takes \(n \ge 2\) values, with probability mass function \(p\). A Huffman code for \(X\) is a binary code built as follows:

Start with \(n\) nodes, one for each value \(x\), each carrying the number \(p(x)\).
Repeat \(n - 1\) times: take two nodes that carry the smallest numbers, make them the two children of a new node that carries the sum of theirs, and label the edge to one child \(0\) and the edge to the other child \(1\).
Give each value \(x\) the codeword made of the labels on the path from the last node down to the node for \(x\).

Ties between nodes that carry equal numbers may be broken in any way, so \(X\) can have several Huffman codes.











Theorem 3 (Huffman codes are prefix codes) Every Huffman code is a prefix code.










ProofProof






Proof. The construction in Definition 2 builds a tree whose nodes for the values \(x\) are leaves: each of them is made first, and only the new nodes get children. The codeword \(c(x)\) is the list of edge labels on the path from the last node to the leaf for \(x\).
Suppose that \(c(x)\) were the beginning of \(c(x')\) for two different values \(x\) and \(x'\). Both paths start at the last node, and the same labels lead to the same child at every step, so the path to \(x\) would be the first part of the path to \(x'\). Then the leaf for \(x\) would lie on the way to the leaf for \(x'\), and the leaf for \(x\) would have a child. No leaf has a child, so no codeword is the beginning of another.











Example 2 (A Huffman code for a five-valued variable)  

Let \(X\) have five values with probability mass function \(p = (0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)\). The code below carries out the construction of Definition 2, breaking ties in favor of the node listed first. It then computes the expected length \(L\) of the code, the entropy \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) with base-2 logarithms, and the sum \({s_{x}} 2^{-\ell(x)}\) of Theorem 1.


Show code
huffman_code <- function(p) {
  codewords <- rep("", length(p))
  weights <- p
  members <- as.list(seq_along(p))
  while (length(weights) > 1) {
    ord <- order(weights)
    first <- ord[1]
    second <- ord[2]
    low <- members[[first]]
    high <- members[[second]]
    codewords[low] <- paste0("0", codewords[low])
    codewords[high] <- paste0("1", codewords[high])
    merged_weight <- weights[first] + weights[second]
    merged_members <- c(low, high)
    two_smallest <- 1:2
    rest <- ord[-two_smallest]
    weights <- c(weights[rest], merged_weight)
    members <- c(members[rest], list(merged_members))
  }
  codewords
}
p <- c(0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)
codewords <- huffman_code(p)
len <- nchar(codewords)
surprisal <- -log2(p)
expected_length <- sum(p * len)
entropy <- sum(p * surprisal)
kraft_sum <- sum(2^(-len))
data.frame(p = p, codeword = codewords, length = len)



  



Show code
c(expected_length = expected_length, entropy = entropy, kraft_sum = kraft_sum)
#> expected_length         entropy       kraft_sum 
#>        2.200000        2.121928        1.000000


The code has expected length \(L = 2.2\) bits and the source has entropy \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = 2.122\) bits, so \(L - {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = 0.078\) bits. The sum \({s_{x}} 2^{-\ell(x)} = 1\) is the largest value Theorem 1 allows, and no codeword is the beginning of another, as Theorem 3 says.

title: Huffman codes
text:
3 Optimality








Theorem 4 (Huffman codes are optimal) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable that takes \(n \ge 2\) values, each with probability \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} > 0\). Then a Huffman code for \(X\) has the least expected length \(L\) among all prefix codes for \(X\).










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction on \(n\). For \(n = 2\), every prefix code gives each value a codeword of at least one bit, and the Huffman code gives them the codewords \(0\) and \(1\), so no prefix code is shorter.
Let \(n > 2\), and suppose the claim holds for \(n - 1\) values. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be two values with the smallest probabilities, the pair that the first step of the construction merges.
First, some prefix code with the least expected length has \(x\) and \(y\) as siblings, meaning that their codewords have the same length \(m\) and differ only in the last bit. To see this, take a prefix code with the least expected length.

If \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(u\right)\mathclose{}} > {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(v\right)\mathclose{}}\), then \({\ell\mathopen{}\left(u\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\ell\mathopen{}\left(v\right)\mathclose{}}\). Otherwise, exchanging the codewords of \(u\) and \(v\) changes \(L\) by \(({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(u\right)\mathclose{}} - {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(v\right)\mathclose{}})({\ell\mathopen{}\left(v\right)\mathclose{}} - {\ell\mathopen{}\left(u\right)\mathclose{}}) < 0\).
A longest codeword \(c\) has a sibling. Otherwise, deleting the last bit of \(c\) leaves a string that neither begins another codeword nor is begun by one, which gives a prefix code with a smaller \(L\).

Let \(u\) be a value with a longest codeword, and let \(v\) be the value of its sibling. Both codewords have length \(m\), the largest codeword length. By the first bullet, exchanging the codeword of \(x\) with that of \(u\) does not increase \(L\), because \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(u\right)\mathclose{}}\) and \({\ell\mathopen{}\left(u\right)\mathclose{}} = m\) is the largest length. The same holds for exchanging \(y\) with \(v\). If \(x\) or \(y\) is already one of \(u\) and \(v\), leave it where it is, and exchange the other with the remaining one of the pair. If \(x = v\) and \(y \ne u\), for example, exchange \(y\) with \(u\). Ties among the smallest probabilities do not matter, because every value other than \(x\) and \(y\) has probability at least \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{}}\), and the exchanges use only that. These exchanges give a prefix code with the least expected length in which \(x\) and \(y\) are siblings.
Next, let \(X'\) be the random variable that merges \(x\) and \(y\) into one value \(z\) with \(\mathbb{p}'\mathopen{}\left(z\right)\mathclose{} = {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{}}\) and keeps every other value and probability. Any prefix code for \(X\) in which \(x\) and \(y\) are siblings turns into a prefix code for \(X'\) by deleting the last bit of their common codeword to make the codeword of \(z\). The two codes differ only in the lengths of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), so their expected lengths satisfy
\[L= L' + {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} + {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
The Huffman code for \(X\) is built from a Huffman code for \(X'\) by replacing the codeword of \(z\) with two codewords, one that ends in \(0\) and one that ends in \(1\). By the induction hypothesis, a Huffman code for \(X'\) has the least expected length \(L'\) among prefix codes for \(X'\). So no prefix code for \(X\) in which \(x\) and \(y\) are siblings has an expected length below that of the Huffman code for \(X\). By the first part, a prefix code with the least expected length is among these, so the Huffman code has the least expected length among all prefix codes.











Example 3 (Three prefix codes for one source)  

Take the source of Example 2, with probabilities \((0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)\). Its Huffman code has the codeword lengths \((2, 2, 2, 3, 3)\). A fixed-length code gives every value three bits. Giving each value \(x\) the length \({\mathopen{}\left\lceil-\log_2 {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\rceil\mathclose{}}\) is a third choice of lengths. All three choices satisfy the sum in Theorem 1, so Theorem 2 gives a prefix code for each. The code below computes their expected lengths.


Show code
p <- c(0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)
huffman_lengths <- c(2, 2, 2, 3, 3)
fixed_lengths <- rep(3, length(p))
shannon_lengths <- ceiling(-log2(p))
length_sets <- list(huffman_lengths, fixed_lengths, shannon_lengths)
data.frame(
  code = c("Huffman", "fixed length", "Shannon lengths"),
  kraft_sum = vapply(length_sets, function(l) sum(2^(-l)), numeric(1)),
  expected_length = vapply(length_sets, function(l) sum(p * l), numeric(1))
)



  



The Huffman code has the least expected length of the three, as Theorem 4 says it must have among all prefix codes.











Theorem 5 (A Huffman code is within one bit of the entropy) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable that takes \(n \ge 2\) values, each with probability \({\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} > 0\). Then a Huffman code for \(X\) has expected length \(L\) with
\[{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \le L< {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} + 1,\]
where \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) is the entropy of \(X\) with base-2 logarithms.










ProofProof






Proof. Every prefix code is uniquely decodable, so the source coding theorem gives \(L\ge {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\).
For the other half of the claim, give each value \(x\) the length \({\ell\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\lceil-\log_2 {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\rceil\mathclose{}}\). Then \(2^{-{\ell\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}} \le {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\), so adding \(2^{-{\ell\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}}\) for every value gives at most the sum of their probabilities, which is \(1\). By Theorem 2, some prefix code has these lengths. Its expected length is below \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} + 1\), because \({\ell\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} < -\log_2 {\mathbb{p}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} + 1\) for each value.
By Theorem 4, a Huffman code has an expected length no larger than this prefix code, so \(L< {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} + 1\).











Example 4 (The bound for the Huffman code of the earlier example)  

The Huffman code of Example 2 has the codeword lengths \((2, 2, 2, 3, 3)\) for the probabilities \((0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)\). The code below computes its entropy and expected length.


Show code
p <- c(0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)
huffman_lengths <- c(2, 2, 2, 3, 3)
entropy <- -sum(p * log2(p))
expected_length <- sum(p * huffman_lengths)
data.frame(entropy, expected_length, upper_bound = entropy + 1)



  



The expected length is \(2.2\) bits. It lies between the entropy, \(2.122\) bits, and the entropy plus one bit, \(3.122\) bits, as Theorem 5 says.

title: Entropy and mutual information
text: This page builds on the definitions of entropy, cross-entropy and Kullback–Leibler divergence in Probability for Data Science.

title: Entropy and mutual information
text:
1 Surprisal








Definition 1 (Surprisal) The surprisal of a value \(x\) of a discrete random variable \(X\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) > 0\) is
\[s(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}-\log \mathbb{P}(X=x).\]
With base-2 logarithms, surprisal is also called the Shannon information content of the value \(x\) (MacKay 2003, sec. 2.4).











Definition 2 (Bit (shannon)) A bit, also called a shannon (symbol Sh) (International Electrotechnical Commission 2008), is the unit of information when the logarithm in surprisal, and in every quantity built from it, has base \(2\).
One bit is the surprisal of a value with probability \(1/2\): for a value \(x\) of a discrete random variable \(X\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(x) = 1 \text{ bit}
&\iff -\log_2 \mathbb{P}(X=x) = 1\\
&\iff \mathbb{P}(X=x) = 2^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In words, a bit is the surprisal of the outcome of one trial whose two outcomes are equally likely, such as one toss of a fair coin.











Example 1 (Counting bits with fair coins) One toss of a fair coin has \(2\) equally likely outcomes, and one binary digit is enough to record which one happened. Two tosses have \(4\) outcomes, and two binary digits record them. In general, \(k\) tosses have \(n = 2^k\) equally likely outcomes, and \(k = \log_2 n\) binary digits record them.
Each of those \(n\) outcomes has probability \(p = 1/n\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
k
&= \log_2 n \\
&= \log_2 \frac{1}{p} \\
&= -\log_2 p,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the surprisal of any one of them, in bits.
Ten tosses that all land heads have probability \(2^{-10}\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(\text{ten heads})
&= -\log_2 2^{-10} \\
&= 10 \text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]











Theorem 1 (Surprisal as a logarithm to base one half) For a value \(x\) of a discrete random variable \(X\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) > 0\), the surprisal in bits is
\[s(x) = \log_{1/2} \mathbb{P}(X=x).\]










ProofProof






Proof. Write \(p = \mathbb{P}(X=x)\). The change of base formula gives
\[\log_b y = \frac{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{y\right\}\mathclose{}}}{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{b\right\}\mathclose{}}}\]
for \(y > 0\) and \(b > 0\) with \(b \ne 1\). With \(b = 1/2\) and \(y = p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_{1/2} p
&= \frac{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{p\right\}\mathclose{}}}{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{1/2\right\}\mathclose{}}} \\
&= \frac{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{p\right\}\mathclose{}}}{-{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}} \\
&= -\frac{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{p\right\}\mathclose{}}}{{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}} \\
&= -\log_2 p \\
&= s(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The step from the third to the fourth line is the change of base formula with \(b = 2\).











Example 2 (Halvings of certainty for a loaded coin)  

A coin lands heads with probability \(0.2\). The chunk computes the surprisal of heads in two ways: as \(-\log_2 0.2\), and as \(\log_{1/2} 0.2\).


Show code
p_heads <- 0.2
from_base_two <- -log(x = p_heads, base = 2)
from_base_half <- log(x = p_heads, base = 0.5)
c(from_base_two, from_base_half)
#> [1] 2.321928 2.321928


Both give \(2.322\) bits (Theorem 1). Halving \(1\) that many times gives \(0.5^{2.322} = 0.2\), the probability of heads.











Remark 1 (Surprisal as halvings of certainty). Start from certainty, probability \(1\). Each halving multiplies the probability by \(1/2\). After \(s\) halvings the probability is \((1/2)^s\), and solving \((1/2)^s = p\) for \(s\) gives \(s = \log_{1/2} p\). This count is only motivation. Theorem 1 proves that this \(s\) is the surprisal in bits. So the surprisal of a value is the number of times certainty must be halved to reach the probability of that value. When \(p\) is not \((1/2)^k\) for a whole number \(k\), the number of halvings is not a whole number.











Definition 3 (Nat) A nat is the unit of information when the logarithm in surprisal, and in every quantity built from it, is the natural logarithm.
One nat is the surprisal of a value with probability \(1/\text{e}\): for a value \(x\) of a discrete random variable \(X\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(x) = 1 \text{ nat}
&\iff -\ln \mathbb{P}(X=x) = 1\\
&\iff \mathbb{P}(X=x) = \text{e}^{-1} = 1/\text{e}\approx 0.368.
\end{aligned}
\]











Example 3 (One fair coin toss in nats) By Example 1 with \(k = 1\), one toss of a fair coin landing heads has a surprisal of \(1\) bit. In nats, the same outcome has a surprisal of
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(\text{heads})
&= -\ln \tfrac{1}{2} \\
&= \ln 2 \\
&\approx 0.693 \text{ nats}.
\end{aligned}
\]











Remark 2 (Converting between bits and nats). For any probability \(p \in (0, 1]\), the change-of-base rule for logarithms gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\log_2 p
&= \frac{-\ln p}{\ln 2}\\
&\approx 1.443 \times (-\ln p).
\end{aligned}
\]
So a value with a surprisal of \(1\) nat has a surprisal of \(1 / \ln 2 \approx 1.443\) bits, and the \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\) nats of Example 3 are exactly \(\ln 2 / \ln 2 = 1\) bit.
A bit as a unit of information is not the same thing as a bit as a binary digit. The name shannon refers only to the unit of information, so it avoids this ambiguity. A binary digit whose two values are equally likely has a surprisal of exactly \(1\) bit, whichever value it takes. A binary digit that is \(0\) nine times in ten does not: the value \(0\) has a surprisal of \(-\log_2 0.9 \approx 0.152\) bits, and the value \(1\) has a surprisal of \(-\log_2 0.1 \approx 3.322\) bits.











Remark 3 (Unlikely outcomes carry more information). The surprisal of a value is large when the value was unlikely, and it falls to \(0\) as the value becomes certain. Correctly guessing heads on one toss of a fair coin is worth \(1\) bit; correctly guessing ten heads in a row is worth \(10\) bits.











Remark 4 (Entropy is expected surprisal). The entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the expectation of its surprisal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X)
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[-\log \mathbb{P}(X)\right]\mathclose{}} \\
&= {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[s(X)\right]\mathclose{}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(H(X)\) is the average number of bits (with base-2 logarithms) needed to record a value of \(X\) when each value \(x\) costs \(s(x)\) bits. The source coding theorem, on a later page of these notes, makes that average precise: no uniquely decodable code does better.











Definition 4 (Rarity) The rarity of a value \(x\) of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the reciprocal of its probability mass:
\[{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}(X=x)}.\]
For a continuous random variable \(X\) with density \(\mathbb{p}\), the rarity of a value \(x\) is the reciprocal of the density:
\[{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\frac{1}{\mathbb{p}(x)}.\]
When the mass or the density is \(0\), the rarity is \(\infty\).











Example 4 (Rarity of the outcomes of a die)  

Let \(X\) be the roll of a fair six-sided die. Each outcome has probability \(1/6\).


Show code
rarity <- function(p) 1 / p
p_fair <- 1 / 6
p_loaded_six <- 1 / 2
p_loaded_other <- (1 - p_loaded_six) / 5
rarity_fair <- rarity(p_fair)
rarity_loaded_six <- rarity(p_loaded_six)
rarity_loaded_other <- rarity(p_loaded_other)
rarities <- c(
  fair = rarity_fair,
  loaded_six = rarity_loaded_six,
  loaded_other = rarity_loaded_other
)
rarities
#>         fair   loaded_six loaded_other 
#>            6            2           10


So each face of the fair die has rarity \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = 6\): one roll in six.
Suppose the die is loaded so that a six has probability \(1/2\). Then \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(6\right)\mathclose{}} = 2\). If the other five faces share the rest equally, each has \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = 10\). The more probable an outcome, the lower its rarity.











Remark 5 (Source of the name). Leinster writes that, for a community whose \(i\)th species has relative abundance \(p_i\), “\(1/p_i\) is a measure of its rarity or specialness”  (Leinster 2021, sec. 2.4, p. 52). The name “rarity” for the reciprocal of a probability is borrowed from there.











Theorem 2 (Surprisal is the logarithm of the rarity) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable, and let \(x\) be a value of \(X\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) > 0\). Then the surprisal of \(x\) is the logarithm of its rarity:
\[{\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}
&= -{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathbb{P}(X=x)\right\}\mathclose{}} && \text{(definition of surprisal)} \\
&= {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}(X=x)}\right\}\mathclose{}} && \text{(logarithm of a reciprocal)} \\
&= {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}. && \text{(definition of rarity)}
\end{aligned}
\]











Theorem 3 (Surprisal of a continuous value is the logarithm of the rarity) Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with density \(\mathbb{p}\), and let \(x\) be a value with \(\mathbb{p}(x) > 0\). Then the surprisal of \(x\) is the logarithm of its rarity:
\[{\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}
&= -{\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathbb{p}(x)\right\}\mathclose{}} && \text{(definition of surprisal)} \\
&= {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\frac{1}{\mathbb{p}(x)}\right\}\mathclose{}} && \text{(logarithm of a reciprocal)} \\
&= {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}. && \text{(definition of rarity)}
\end{aligned}
\]











Corollary 1 (Surprisal of a discrete value is nonnegative) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable, and let \(x\) be a value of \(X\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) > 0\). Then the rarity of \(x\) is at least \(1\), with equality exactly when \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) = 1\), and the surprisal satisfies
\[{\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} \ge 0.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Since \(0 < \mathbb{P}(X=x) \le 1\), the rarity \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = 1 / \mathbb{P}(X=x)\) is at least \(1\), with equality exactly when \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) = 1\). The logarithm is increasing, and \({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} = 0\), so by Theorem 2, \({\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = {\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} \ge 0\).











Example 5 (Surprisal and rarity of a value with probability one quarter) Take a value with probability \(1/4\):

rarity_four <- 1 / p_four
surprisal_four <- log2(rarity_four)
surprisal_four
#> [1] 2


It has rarity \(4\) by definition. By Theorem 2, its surprisal is the base-2 logarithm of that rarity, \(2\) bits.












Remark 6 (Reading the rarity of a value). A density can exceed \(1\), so for a continuous random variable the rarity can be below \(1\), and then the surprisal is negative (Theorem 3). For a mass, a rarity of \(r\) reads “one in \(r\)”, and the surprisal is the logarithm of \(r\) (Theorem 2).











Remark 7 (Values of the probability, the rarity and the surprisal). For a discrete random variable, the mass \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) of a value with a mass above \(0\), its rarity \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) and its surprisal \({\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) take the values in the middle column. For a continuous random variable, the density \(\mathbb{p}(x)\) takes the place of the mass. At a value \(x\) with a density above \(0\), the rarity \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) is the reciprocal of \(\mathbb{p}(x)\), and the surprisal \({\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) is the surprisal of a continuous value. Their values are in the right column.

Mass. A mass of \(1\) gives the smallest rarity, \(1\), and the smallest surprisal, \(0\). No mass exceeds \(1\), the probability of a value that is certain. So no mass gives a rarity below \(1\) or a surprisal below \(0\).
Density. A density can be arbitrarily large, as in the uniform example, so the rarity can fall below \(1\) and the surprisal can fall below \(0\).
Zero. A mass or density of \(0\) gives a rarity and a surprisal of \(\infty\).
Units. A mass has no units. A density has the units of \(1/x\), so its rarity has the units of \(x\). Rescaling \(x\) by a nonzero \(c\) shifts its surprisal by \({\operatorname{log}\mathopen{}\left\{\mathopen{}\left|c\right|\mathclose{}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).












Remark 8 (Rarity and odds). Let \(x\) be a value of a discrete random variable \(X\), and let \(A\) be the event \(X = x\) with probability \(p = \mathbb{P}(X=x)\). The odds in favour of \(A\) are \(p / (1 - p)\), and the odds against \(A\) are \((1 - p) / p\) (Grinstead and Snell 1997, Definition 1.4). The rarity of \(x\) is \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} = 1/p\), so the odds against \(A\) are \({\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}} - 1\).


Show code
p_value <- c(1 / 4, 1 / 100, 1)
rarity_value <- 1 / p_value
odds_against <- (1 - p_value) / p_value
rarity_value - odds_against
#> [1] 1 1 1
rarity_value
#> [1]   4 100   1
odds_against
#> [1]  3 99  0


The first printed line shows that, for each \(p\), the rarity of the value exceeds the odds against its event by exactly \(1\). A value with probability \(1/4\) has rarity \(4\), and its event has odds of \(3\) to \(1\) against. The two differ by exactly \(1\), so they are relatively close when the rarity is large. At \(p = 1\) the rarity is \(1\) and the odds against are \(0\), but the odds in favour divide by zero.
The odds compare an event with its complement, and the odds against take values in \([0, \infty)\) when \(p\) is above \(0\). At \(p = 0\), the odds against and the rarity divide by zero, and both tend to \(\infty\) as \(p\) decreases to \(0\). For a value of a discrete random variable with \(p\) above \(0\), the rarity takes values in \([1, \infty)\). For a continuous random variable, the event \(X = x\) for a single value has probability \(0\), so its odds against and \(1/\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) are not defined, but the rarity of the value is defined from the density. An event such as \(X \le c\) can have a probability above \(0\), so it can have odds.











Definition 5 (Perplexity) The perplexity of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the exponential of its entropy, with the same base as the logarithm in the entropy:
\[{\mathrm{PP}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}b^{{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}}.\]
With base-2 logarithms, \({\mathrm{PP}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = 2^{{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}}\) with \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) in bits. With natural logarithms, \({\mathrm{PP}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = \text{e}^{{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}}\) with \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) in nats. The two give the same value.











Theorem 4 (Perplexity is the probability-weighted geometric mean of the rarities) For a discrete random variable \(X\), the perplexity is a weighted geometric mean  of the rarities, each raised to its probability. Take \(x\) over the values with \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) > 0\). Then
\[{\mathrm{PP}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = \prod_x {\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}^{\mathbb{P}(X=x)}.\]










ProofProof






Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathrm{PP}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}
&= b^{{\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}}
&& \text{(definition of perplexity)} \\
&= b^{{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}}}
&& \text{(entropy is expected surprisal)} \\
&= b^{\sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x) \log_b {\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}}
&& \text{(surprisal is the logarithm of the rarity)} \\
&= \prod_x b^{\mathbb{P}(X=x) \log_b {\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}}
&& \text{(a sum in the exponent is a product)} \\
&= \prod_x {\mathbb{r}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}^{\mathbb{P}(X=x)}
&& \text{(} b^{\log_b y} = y \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]











Example 6 (Perplexity of a uniform distribution)  

If \(X\) is uniform on \(k\) values, then every value has probability \(1/k\) and rarity \(k\), so by Theorem 4 the perplexity of \(X\) is \(k\). In general, the perplexity is the count of equally likely values that would give the same entropy as \(X\).











Example 7 (Perplexity of a loaded die)  

Let \(X\) be the roll of the loaded die from Example 4, where a six has probability \(1/2\) and each other face has probability \(1/10\). The code computes the perplexity from the entropy in bits, and then from the rarities by Theorem 4.


Show code
p_other_faces <- rep(1 / 10, 5)
p <- c(1 / 2, p_other_faces)
surprisal <- -log2(p)
entropy <- sum(p * surprisal)
perplexity_from_entropy <- 2^entropy
rarity <- 1 / p
perplexity_from_rarities <- prod(rarity^p)
c(perplexity_from_entropy, perplexity_from_rarities)
#> [1] 4.472136 4.472136


Both routes give a perplexity of about \(4.47\). The loaded die has the same entropy as a fair die with about that many faces, fewer than the \(6\) faces it has.











Remark 9 (Source of the name). The name comes from speech recognition (Jelinek et al. 1977). Leinster defines the “diversity of order 1” as the exponential of the entropy (Leinster 2021, Definition 2.4.1). He calls a diversity index an “effective number” when it is \(k\) for \(k\) species with the same abundance (Leinster 2021, Definition 2.4.5).











Remark 10 (Differential entropy differs from entropy). A density value is not a probability, so the surprisal of a continuous value and the entropy of a continuous random variable (the differential entropy) behave differently from their counterparts for a discrete random variable:

Sign. A density can exceed \(1\), so the surprisal \({\mathbb{s}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) and the differential entropy can fall below \(0\), as in the uniform example (Cover and Thomas 2006, sec. 8.1). The entropy of a discrete random variable is never negative.
Units. Rescaling changes the differential entropy: \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(aX\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} + \log |a|\) for a constant \(a \ne 0\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, Theorem 8.6.4). Measuring the same quantity in metres rather than centimetres therefore changes it. Adding a constant does not: \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X + c\right)\mathclose{}} = {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, Theorem 8.6.3).
Not what the entropy approaches. Round \(X\) down to a multiple of \(\Delta\), which gives a discrete random variable \(X^\Delta\). Then \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X^\Delta\right)\mathclose{}} + \log \Delta \to {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) as \(\Delta \to 0\) (Cover and Thomas 2006, Theorem 8.3.1). The entropy \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X^\Delta\right)\mathclose{}}\) itself grows indefinitely as \(\Delta \to 0\), so the differential entropy is not what it approaches.












Definition 6 (Collision probability) The collision probability of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the chance that \(X\) and a second variable \(X'\) take the same value, where \(X\) and \(X'\) are IID:
\[\mathbb{P}(X = X').\]











Definition 7 (Rényi entropy of order 2 (collision entropy)) The Rényi entropy of order 2, also called the collision entropy (Wikipedia contributors 2026), of a discrete random variable \(X\) is the negative logarithm of the expectation of its probability,  where \({\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) is the probability mass function evaluated at the random variable \(X\) itself:
\[{\mathbb{H}_{2}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} = -\log {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}}.\]
Rényi introduced this case of a family of entropies (Rényi 1961).











Theorem 5 (The expected probability is the collision probability) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable, and let \(X'\) be a variable such that \(X\) and \(X'\) are IID. Then
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathbb{P}(X)\right]\mathclose{}} = \sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x)^2 = \mathbb{P}(X = X').\]










ProofProof






Proof. The expectation of \(\mathbb{P}(X)\) adds, over the values \(x\), the value \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) times its probability \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathbb{P}(X)\right]\mathclose{}}
&= \sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x) \, \mathbb{P}(X=x) \\
&= \sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The variables \(X\) and \(X'\) take the same value exactly when both equal some value \(x\). Because \(X\) and \(X'\) are IID, the probability that both equal \(x\) is \(\mathbb{P}(X=x) \, \mathbb{P}(X'=x) = \mathbb{P}(X=x)^2\). Adding over the values \(x\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X = X')
&= \sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x, X'=x) \\
&= \sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The expectation \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathbb{P}(X)\right]\mathclose{}}\) and the collision probability \(\mathbb{P}(X = X')\) both equal \(\sum_x \mathbb{P}(X=x)^2\), so they are equal.











Theorem 6 (The collision entropy is at most the Shannon entropy) Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable with values \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\). Then the collision entropy is at most the entropy:
\[{\mathbb{H}_{2}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}} \le {\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}.\]
The two coincide exactly when each value that \(X\) takes with positive probability has the same probability.










ProofProof






Proof. Write \({\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) for the probability mass function evaluated at \(X\). The function \(-\log\) is strictly convex, so Jensen’s inequality gives
\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[-\log {\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}} \ge -\log {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[{\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\right]\mathclose{}},\]
with equality exactly when \({\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) is constant. The left side is \({\mathbb{H}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\). The right side is \({\mathbb{H}_{2}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) by its definition. The function \({\mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{}}\) is constant exactly when every value that \(X\) takes with positive probability has that same probability. 











Example 8 (Collision entropy and entropy of a three-valued random variable)  

Let \(X\) take three values with probabilities \(1/2\), \(1/4\) and \(1/4\). The code below computes the expected probability, the collision entropy and the entropy, with base-2 logarithms.
